prompt.context: Our company is a manufacturing business in the Southeastern U.S. We have a number of salespeople who are consistently reimbursed for gas. We would like to determine how much we spent on gasoline last year so that we can evaluate how the rising cost of gasoline will impact our bottom line.
prompt.question: Question 1: What was the cost of gas last year? Question 2: How will our expenses be affected going forward? Question 3: Do you have any recommendations on what we can do to curb our expenses?

clarifying_info.q: How many salespeople do we have?
clarifying_info.a: 30 salespeople spread throughout the country, in 3 regions — East, Central, West — with 10 per region.

clarifying_info.q: How much does a typical salesperson drive?
clarifying_info.a: 1000 miles per week on average, but there are three driver categories: low (500 miles/week), medium (1000 miles/week), and high (1500 miles/week). There are 5 low, 15 medium, and 10 high mileage drivers.

clarifying_info.q: Do salespeople get reimbursed for personal use?
clarifying_info.a: They are not supposed to, but it does happen.

clarifying_info.q: What is the fuel efficiency of the vehicles?
Are there other uses of gasoline (delivery trucks, factory machines, etc.)?
clarifying_info.a: There are, but do not worry about them for this case.

clarifying_info.q: Are there plans to change the sales force size or driving habits next year?
clarifying_info.a: No change in habits or mileage is planned.

framework: Determine total annual miles driven by all salespeople (segment by driver category)
Multiply gallons by average gas price per gallon to get annual cost
Consider quarterly breakdowns to capture gas price variation throughout the year
Build in a cushion for personal usage that slips through reimbursement controls
For forward-looking impact, develop 3 scenarios (worst, best, most likely) based on projected gas prices
Generate recommendations to control and reduce gas reimbursement expenses

questions.prompt: Calculate the total annual gasoline cost for last year.
questions.guidance: Candidate should segment drivers into the three categories, calculate total miles per week per category, sum to total fleet miles per week, annualize, divide by MPG to get gallons, and multiply by an assumed average gas price. A strong answer notes the need to account for personal use leakage and considers using quarterly price averages rather than a single annual price.

math.setup: Driver segments: 5 low (500 mi/wk), 15 medium (1000 mi/wk), 10 high (1500 mi/wk). Vehicles = 30 MPG. Candidate must assume an average gas price (e.g. $2.50/gallon).
math.answer: Approximately $140,000–$155,000 per year (at ~$2.50/gal), before or after personal-use cushion; exact figure depends on assumed gas price and personal-use adjustment.

questions.prompt: How will our gasoline expenses be affected going forward (next year)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should develop three scenarios — best case (gas price falls), most likely (gas prices rise moderately), and worst case (sharp price increase) — and calculate the expense impact for each using the same mileage base. No change in driving habits or headcount is assumed.

math.setup: Same annual gallons ≈ 56,333. Model three gas price assumptions.
math.answer: Expenses range from ~$113K (best) to ~$197K (worst), with ~$155K most likely — representing a significant increase vs. prior year if prices rise.

brainstorming.prompt: What recommendations can you make to keep gasoline reimbursement expenses down?

categories.name: Cost Controls & Policies
ideas: Set mileage or dollar caps on weekly/monthly reimbursements
Reimburse only for one octane level (regular unleaded)
Require prior approval for trips above a mileage threshold
Enforce strict separation of personal vs. business mileage (e.g. mileage logs)

categories.name: Visibility & Tracking Tools
ideas: Issue company gas cards to capture transaction-level data
Use GPS or telematics to track actual business miles driven
Require electronic mileage submission with manager sign-off

categories.name: Financial Risk Management
ideas: Hedge fuel costs using oil futures or options contracts
Lock in fuel prices via bulk purchasing agreements with a fuel supplier

categories.name: Operational Efficiency
ideas: Optimize sales territories to reduce average drive distances
Encourage carpooling or shared trips for salespeople in the same region
Shift some customer interactions to phone/video to reduce drive frequency
Replace high-mileage vehicles with more fuel-efficient models

recommendation: Last year's gasoline expense was approximately $140K–$155K (at ~$2.50/gal) driven by 30 salespeople across three mileage tiers covering roughly 1.69M miles annually.
Under a likely moderate price increase scenario, annual costs could rise to ~$155K–$197K, representing material P&L exposure as gas prices continue rising.
Immediate priority should be implementing gas cards and mileage tracking for full visibility, combined with reimbursement caps and a policy to reimburse only regular-grade fuel.
risks: Personal use of company-reimbursed gas is already occurring and understated in current figures — actual spend may be higher.
If gas prices spike (worst-case $3.50+), costs could approach $200K+ annually with no mechanism to cap exposure.
A rigid cap policy without flexibility may hurt salesperson morale or reduce customer coverage.
next_steps: Deploy company-issued gas cards within 30 days to gain transaction visibility.
Formalize a reimbursement policy with mileage tiers and a per-trip approval process.
Evaluate a fuel price hedging strategy with the CFO if oil price volatility remains high.
Conduct a territory optimization exercise to reduce average miles per salesperson.
